🏗️ Semantic HTML

Which element to reach for, and why every component here emits landmarks and headings rather than a nest of anonymous boxes. A tag is the cheapest accessibility and SEO work available: it costs nothing at runtime, and no amount of ARIA bought later replaces it.

The same layout, twice

Both trees render identically. Only one of them tells a browser, a screen reader or a crawler what any of it means. The left is flat grey on purpose — an undifferentiated tree is the whole point.

Non-Semantic HTML
<div>
<span>
<div>
<div>
<div>
<div>
<div>
<div>
Semantic HTML
<header>
<nav>
<aside>
<main>
<article>
<figure>
<p>
<section>
<footer>

The page skeleton, with this system's components

No component in this library renders a page-level landmark it cannot own. TopNav and ProductMenu each emit their own <nav> but neither emits <header> — two headers would be wrong, and only the page knows it is a page. Wrap them yourself.

<body>
  <header>                          <!-- the page's banner: both strips live here -->
    <TopNav items={…} />            <!-- emits <nav aria-label="Corporate"> -->
    <ProductMenu … />               <!-- emits <nav aria-label="Product">   -->
  </header>

  <main>                            <!-- exactly one per page, never nested -->
    <h1>IronPDF for .NET</h1>       <!-- exactly one h1, and it is the subject -->

    <article>                       <!-- stands alone: a post, a product, a card -->
      <h2>Convert HTML to PDF</h2>
      <figure>
        <img src="…" alt="…">
        <figcaption>Output at 300 dpi</figcaption>
      </figure>
      <p>…</p>
    </article>

    <section aria-labelledby="pricing">   <!-- a themed group; name it -->
      <h2 id="pricing">Pricing</h2>
      <TrialKeyCard … />            <!-- emits its own <form> -->
    </section>
  </main>

  <aside aria-label="Related">      <!-- tangential to the page, not to <main> -->
    <Notice … />
  </aside>

  <footer>                          <!-- the page's footer, once -->
    <Footer products={…} />         <!-- a <section>: it is a band, not the footer -->
    <FooterBar />                   <!-- already a <footer>; do not double-wrap -->
  </footer>
</body>

Element reference

The column that saves the most time is the last one. Most misuse is not reaching for a tag that does not exist — it is reaching for one that means something else.

ElementUse it forNot for
<header>The banner of a page — or of an article/section, where it is scoped rather than a landmark.Any box that happens to sit at the top.
<nav>A major block of navigation links. Give each one an aria-label when a page has more than one.Every group of links. A footer's legal links do not need one.
<main>The page's unique content. Exactly one, not nested in any other landmark.A content column that repeats across pages.
<article>Something that would still make sense pulled out and shown alone — a post, a product row, a comment.A generic card. If it only makes sense in place, it is a section.
<section>A themed group of content that has, or could have, a heading. Name it with aria-labelledby.A styling wrapper. An unnamed section is a div with extra steps.
<aside>Content tangential to what surrounds it — the spec names call-out boxes explicitly.Any sidebar-shaped thing. A nav sidebar is a nav.
<figure>Referenced content — image, diagram, code sample — with an optional figcaption.Every image. A decorative one is an img alt="".
<address>Contact details for the nearest article or the document. Reset its italics and margins.Any postal address, such as one in a shipping table.
<ul> / <ol>Anything the eye reads as a list — including a run of items with dots between them.Layout. A grid of cards is still a list if the cards are peers.
<strong>Text that carries more importance than its surroundings.Text that is merely bold. Inside a heading, use <b>.
<b>Text set apart stylistically with no added importance — a keyword, a product half in a lockup.Emphasis. That is <strong> or <em>.
<div> / <span>Styling and layout hooks with no meaning to convey. Still the right answer, often.Anything the list above already names.

What this library got wrong

Every pair below is a real change made to these components. They are here because they are the mistakes worth recognising, not because they were unusual.

Ten links that were not links Footer.astro
<li class="fp-row"> <span>IRONPDF</span> <span>Create, read and edit PDFs.</span> </li> /* css */ .fp-row { cursor: pointer; }
<li> <a class="fp-row" href={p.href}> <span>IRONPDF</span> <span>Create, read and edit PDFs.</span> </a> </li>
Why it mattered: href had been in the component's own Product interface since it shipped and was never rendered. A pointer cursor is not a link: ten internal links were invisible to a crawler and unreachable by keyboard. This is the single highest-value fix on the page.
A submit button with no form FormCard.astro · TrialKeyCard.astro
<div class="trial-card"> <input type="email" placeholder="Your Business Email*"> <button type="submit">Get key</button> </div>
<form class="trial-card" action=… method=…> <label class="tc-label" for={id}>…</label> <input id={id} type="email" autocomplete="email" required> <button type="submit">Get key</button> </form>
Why it mattered: type="submit" outside a form submits nothing — there was no Enter-to-submit and no validation. And a placeholder is not a label: it is not announced by every screen reader, and it disappears the moment the user types, taking the field's only description with it. The label is visually hidden, not removed.
Two <h1>s on 29 pages docs/*.html
<header> <h1>Iron Software Design System</h1> </header> … <div class="page-title"><h1>Badge</h1></div> <div class="sect-h">Preview</div>
<header> <span class="site-name">Iron Software…</span> </header> … <div class="page-title"><h1>Badge</h1></div> <h2 class="sect-h">Preview</h2>
Why it mattered: site branding repeated on every page is not that page's main heading. Meanwhile the section headings were <div>s, so pages jumped from h1 straight to h3 with nothing in between. The classes already set font-size, weight and margin, so all 138 swaps were pixel-identical.
A breadcrumb made of text docs/component-*.html
<div class="crumb"> <a href="…">Components</a> &nbsp;/&nbsp; Badge </div>
<nav class="crumb" aria-label="Breadcrumb"> <ol> <li><a href="…">Components</a></li> <li>Badge</li> </ol> </nav>
Why it mattered: the separator moved out of the markup into li + li::before, so it is decoration a screen reader never reads, and the visible trail now mirrors the BreadcrumbList JSON-LD that every component page emits.
Icons that announced themselves 7 SVGs across 5 components
<svg viewBox="0 0 512 512"> <path d="…"/> </svg>
<svg viewBox="0 0 512 512" aria-hidden="true"> <path d="…"/> </svg>
Why it mattered: a decorative SVG with no aria-hidden can be announced as an unnamed graphic beside the text it decorates. 25 of the 32 icons here already had it; the other 7 did not, which is exactly how this kind of gap survives — it looks done.

Rules that are easy to get wrong

Each of these came up while making the changes above.

A component cannot know its heading level

A card hard-coding <h3> breaks the outline everywhere it does not happen to sit under an h2. FormCard, TrialKeyCard and Footer take a headingLevel prop and default to what they rendered before.

An explicit role replaces the implicit one

Notice is an <aside>, but its default role="status" overrides the complementary landmark — so six notices do not add six landmarks. Only live={false} makes one a landmark, which is the case where it genuinely is complementary.

Name a landmark or do not add one

Two unnamed <nav>s are worse than one. Every landmark this library emits carries a name: aria-label="Corporate", "Product", "Footer", "Breadcrumb", and Footer's band takes one as a prop.

Group a separator with what it precedes

In a wrapping row, a separator that is its own flex child gets stranded at the end of a line. Put it inside the item that follows it — the FooterBar menu and the card note rows both do.

Semantic tags cost UA styles

<address> arrives italic, <form> and <p> arrive with margins, a heading arrives bold and resized. The docs get this free from a * reset; a component cannot assume the consumer has one, so it resets its own.

Visually hidden is not display:none

display:none and visibility:hidden remove an element from the accessibility tree too. A label with no room on screen uses the clip pattern: 1×1px, clip-path: inset(50%), still announced.
